title: Which plug trips the breaker?
hook: A heater is running. You plug in one more thing and the lights go out. Which thing?

knows: breakers cut the power when a circuit is overloaded
doesNotKnow: that a breaker limits the total current of everything on its circuit

misconception: A breaker's limit is about how many things are plugged in, not about the total current they draw.
objective: The learner can explain that each device draws watts / volts amps, the breaker counts the total, and so a 1500 W heater (12.5 A) leaves room on a 15 A circuit only for a device under 300 W.

claims.text: On a 120 V circuit a device draws I = P / V: a 1500 W heater draws 12.5 A, a 200 W TV 1.7 A, a 600 W blender 5 A, a 1200 W toaster 10 A.
claims.source: P = V I for a resistive load at its nameplate power: 1500/120 = 12.50, 200/120 = 1.67, 600/120 = 5.00, 1200/120 = 10.00 A (artifacts/scratch/w4phys/check.mjs).

claims.text: With the heater on, adding the 200 W TV makes 14.2 A, under 15 A; adding the 600 W blender makes 17.5 A and the 1200 W toaster 22.5 A, both over.
claims.source: Currents in parallel branches add: 12.5 + 1.67 = 14.17, 12.5 + 5 = 17.5, 12.5 + 10 = 22.5 A. The heater leaves 2.5 A = 300 W of room at 120 V.

claims.text: A breaker counts the total current through its circuit, not the number of plugs: TV, blender and toaster together (16.7 A) are over 15 A even with the heater off.
claims.source: Household outlets on one circuit are in parallel; the breaker carries the sum of branch currents: (200 + 600 + 1200)/120 = 16.67 A. A thermal-magnetic breaker responds to current (UL 489 / IEC 60898 rate breakers in amperes).

claims.text: Model: an ideal breaker that opens the instant the total passes 15 A. Real breakers trip on a time curve: a small overload can take minutes or longer, a big one is fast.
claims.source: Stated in the question and on stage ('ideal 15 A breaker') and in the reveal. Thermal-magnetic breakers have an inverse-time thermal trip and an instantaneous magnetic trip at several times rated current; UL 489 requires tripping at 135% of rating within one hour (for ratings up to 50 A) and much faster at 200%, and allows a breaker to carry 100% indefinitely. So 17.5 A (117%) on a real 15 A breaker may take a long time to trip or hold for a while.

claims.text: The 120 V circuit, 15 A breaker and appliance wattages are illustrative (typical of US homes); devices are treated as drawing their nameplate power steadily.
claims.source: 15 A, 120 V branch circuits are common in US homes (NEC 210.3 rates branch circuits by their overcurrent device); nameplate wattages here are typical round values, not measured appliances. Motors (the blender) draw a brief inrush above their running current, ignored here.

recall.question: On a 230 V circuit with a 10 A breaker, a 2000 W kettle is on. Roughly how many more watts can you add before the total passes 10 A?
recall.why: The breaker counts amps: the kettle draws 2000 / 230 ≈ 8.7 A, leaving about 1.3 A, which is 1.3 × 230 ≈ 300 W.
